gold.title: Gold

price.note: 6.9% below the August peak of about $4,700

gold.headline: Gold reads bearish: real yields and the Fed path outweigh war and fiscal risk.

drivers.name: Real yields
drivers.reading: 10-year TIPS yield 2.66%, +23bp in two weeks.
drivers.why: Gold pays no interest, so higher inflation-adjusted yields raise the cost of holding it.
drivers.source: Treasury TIPS curve via StreetStats, 18 Sep; two-week change from Tipswatch and ECM Source

drivers.name: Fed path
drivers.reading: Fed funds 3.75–4.00%, last move +25bp. 2-year yield 4.67%, +30bp in two weeks.
drivers.why: A tightening Fed and rising 2-year yields pull money toward cash and bonds.
drivers.source: Fed statement and dot plot coverage; 2-year yield from Alpha Vantage, 17 Sep

drivers.name: US dollar
drivers.reading: DXY 100.29, +1.3% in two weeks.
drivers.why: Gold is priced in dollars. A stronger dollar makes it dearer for buyers in other currencies.
drivers.source: DXY 100.29 from FXStreet. Weekly gain of about 1.3% from Trading Economics. The two-week change was not found, so the one-week move is used

drivers.name: Inflation expectations
drivers.reading: 10-year breakeven 2.38%, −2bp in two weeks.
drivers.why: Rising breakevens support gold as an inflation hedge. Steady ones mean yields are rising in real terms, not on inflation fears.
drivers.source: FRED T10YIE via ECM Source and Tipswatch

drivers.name: War and fiscal risk
drivers.reading: US-Iran war and energy shock still in play, with oil easing back toward $100 a barrel and heavy government borrowing.
drivers.why: Conflict and government borrowing worries drive demand for gold as a store of value. This score is entered by hand.
drivers.source: Entered by hand from news coverage

drivers.name: Price vs recent high
drivers.reading: Gold $4,378, 6.9% below its August peak of about $4,700.
drivers.why: Checks whether the market is agreeing with the fundamentals.
drivers.source: Investing.com and Trading Economics, 18 Sep

drivers.name: Fund positioning
drivers.reading: Managed money net long 134,972 contracts, COT index 55 of 100 (positions as of 2026-09-08), −2,690 over four weeks.
drivers.why: Hedge funds already heavily long leave few buyers left, so crowded longs raise downside risk. Crowded shorts raise squeeze risk. Set to contrarian in manual.json.
drivers.source: CFTC Disaggregated report via cotdata.net, positions as of 8 Sep. The 15 Sep report is out but I could not read its figures cleanly

flags: Real yields are at 2.66%, yet gold is only 6.9% below its recent high. Something besides rates is holding the price up. The war and fiscal risk driver is the likely candidate, and it is scored by hand.

nasdaq.title: Nasdaq

price.note: 2.1% below the record close of 27,094 on 2 June

nasdaq.headline: Nasdaq reads bearish: real yields and the Fed path outweigh risk appetite.

drivers.name: Real yields
drivers.reading: 10-year TIPS yield 2.66%, +23bp in two weeks.
drivers.why: Growth stocks are valued on distant earnings. Higher real yields discount those earnings harder.
drivers.source: Treasury TIPS curve via StreetStats, 18 Sep; two-week change from Tipswatch and ECM Source

drivers.name: Fed path
drivers.reading: Fed funds 3.75–4.00%, last move +25bp. 2-year yield 4.67%, +30bp in two weeks.
drivers.why: Tighter policy raises borrowing costs and competes with stocks for money.
drivers.source: Fed statement coverage; 2-year yield from Alpha Vantage, 17 Sep

drivers.name: Risk appetite
drivers.reading: VIX 14.8 (−3.0), high-yield spread 2.76% (+5bp).
drivers.why: Low volatility and tight credit spreads mean investors are comfortable owning risk.
drivers.source: VIX from StreetStats, 18 Sep; high-yield spread from FRED via govspending.org, 15 Sep. Two-week changes are approximate

drivers.name: Net liquidity
drivers.reading: Net liquidity $5,864B, 21st percentile of five years, +69B over four weeks.
drivers.why: Fed assets minus the Treasury cash account and reverse repos. More liquidity has tended to lift risk assets.
drivers.source: Fed H.4.1 via StreetStats and Market Ontology, 16 Sep

drivers.name: Oil and war shock
drivers.reading: WTI $100 a barrel, +0.0% in two weeks. The Iran war and Hormuz shipping attacks keep energy inflation risk alive.
drivers.why: Expensive oil feeds inflation, which keeps the Fed hiking and hurts growth stocks. Gold reads the same war as support.
drivers.source: WTI settle from CNBC, 18 Sep. Two-week change not found, set to zero

drivers.name: Earnings and AI spending
drivers.reading: The AI trade is intact: chipmakers bounced back from a mid-week scare and the Nasdaq led the week. Hyperscalers are funding heavy spending with debt.
drivers.why: The largest stocks are about half the index, so their earnings and AI spending set the tone. This score is entered by hand.
drivers.source: Entered by hand from market coverage

drivers.name: Market breadth
drivers.reading: Leadership is narrow. The Nasdaq rose on the week while the Dow fell for a third week and small caps, industrials and consumer discretionary slid for five or more.
drivers.why: Broad participation makes rallies sturdier. Narrow leadership makes them fragile. This score is entered by hand.
drivers.source: Entered by hand from Investrade and TheStreet coverage

drivers.name: Price vs record high
drivers.reading: Nasdaq Composite 26,523, 2.1% below its record close of 27,094 on 2 June.
drivers.why: Trend confirmation. Trading within a few percent of the record counts as bullish.
drivers.source: Nasdaq Composite close 18 Sep; record from Wikipedia milestones page

drivers.name: Fund positioning
drivers.reading: Leveraged funds net short 14,092 contracts, COT index 82 of 100 (positions as of 2026-09-01), +48,000 over two weeks.
drivers.why: Leveraged funds are often hedging, so this is a noisy signal. Contrarian mode treats a crowded long as a risk and a crowded short as squeeze fuel. Set in manual.json.
drivers.source: CFTC TFF report via thetrading.tools, positions as of 1 Sep. Two reports behind, and the two-week change is approximate

flags: The macro drivers lean bearish, yet the Nasdaq is only 2.1% below its record. The market is looking through higher rates, most likely on AI earnings. That gap can close either way.
Fund positioning is stretched (COT index 82 of 100). Crowded positioning makes sharp reversals more likely.

dxy.title: Dollar (DXY)

price.note: 0.2% below the seven-week high of 100.50 (18 Sep)

dxy.headline: Dollar (DXY) reads bullish: the policy path and US real yields outweigh fiscal worries.

drivers.name: Rate gap vs Europe and Japan
drivers.reading: Fed funds mid 3.88% vs ECB 2.50%, BoJ 1.25%, BoE 3.75%. Weighted by index share, the US rate gap is 1.40 points, +0.04 points over four weeks.
drivers.why: The index is 57.6% euro and 13.6% yen. A wider gap between US rates and theirs pulls money into dollars.
drivers.source: Fed, ECB (2.50%, 10 Sep), BoJ (1.25%, 18 Sep) and BoE (3.75%, held) decisions via FXStreet

drivers.name: Expected policy path
drivers.reading: US 2-year yield +30bp in two weeks. Futures give the Fed better than even odds of another hike on 28 October. The ECB is not expected to move before December, and the BoJ's split vote points to gradual tightening.
drivers.why: Markets trade where central banks are heading, not just where rates are. A Fed priced for more hikes than the ECB and BoJ supports the dollar. The edge is entered by hand.
drivers.source: 2-year yield from Alpha Vantage; rate-hike pricing from FXStreet and CME FedWatch coverage. The edge is entered by hand

drivers.name: US real yields
drivers.reading: 10-year TIPS yield 2.66%, +23bp in two weeks. Higher US real yields draw in foreign money.
drivers.why: Higher inflation-adjusted returns on Treasuries draw in foreign money.
drivers.source: Treasury TIPS curve via StreetStats, 18 Sep

drivers.name: Safe-haven demand
drivers.reading: VIX 14.8 (−3.0), high-yield spread 2.76% (+5bp). Calm markets mean less safe-haven demand for the dollar.
drivers.why: The dollar tends to catch a bid when volatility and credit spreads jump. Calm markets take that support away.
drivers.source: VIX from StreetStats, 18 Sep; high-yield spread from FRED via govspending.org, 15 Sep

drivers.name: Oil shock
drivers.reading: WTI $100 a barrel, +0.0% in two weeks. The US is a net energy exporter, so expensive oil helps the dollar against importers like Europe and Japan. Oil has eased this week.
drivers.why: The US is a net energy exporter. Expensive oil hurts importers like Europe and Japan and helps the dollar against them.
drivers.source: WTI settle from CNBC, 18 Sep. Two-week change not found, set to zero

drivers.name: Fiscal and Fed independence
drivers.reading: The 10-year yield touched 5%, its highest since 2007, on fiscal worries. President Trump is again demanding much lower rates, which raises doubts about Fed independence.
drivers.why: Heavy borrowing and pressure on the Fed can push yields up while the dollar falls. This score is entered by hand.
drivers.source: Entered by hand from FXStreet and market coverage

drivers.name: Growth and data
drivers.reading: The Fed calls the US economy strong and this week's jobs data was firm.
drivers.why: Stronger US data than abroad supports the dollar. This score is entered by hand.
drivers.source: Entered by hand from FXStreet and Zacks coverage

drivers.name: Price trend
drivers.reading: DXY 100.27, 0.2% below its seven-week high of 100.50 (18 Sep), +1.3% over the week.
drivers.why: Trend confirmation. A rising index close to its recent high counts as bullish.
drivers.source: FXStreet, 18 Sep. Weekly change from Trading Economics

flags: Rates and central bank paths favour the dollar, but fiscal worries and pressure on the Fed pull the other way. A sell-America episode would show up as the dollar falling while US yields rise.

compare_note: Gold and the Nasdaq read the same way on real yields and the Fed path. They split on war and oil: what supports gold weighs on the Nasdaq. The dollar is the mirror image on real yields and the Fed path: it gains where both of them lose.
